top3.title: Philadelphia Psychotronic Film Society
top3.venue: PhilaMOCA, 531 N 12th St, Philadelphia, PA 19123
top3.why: PhilaMOCA's monthly Psychotronic Film Society meetup is dedicated to the deliberately weird end of genre cinema — exploitation, horror ephemera, and whatever else doesn't fit a normal repertory slot. This screening also closes voting for the 2026 Psychotronic Awards, so it's a bigger night than the usual meetup. Doors 7:00 PM, screening 7:30; Callowhill, a couple of blocks from the Broad Street Line's Spring Garden stop.

All ages, standing-room general admission. Fishtown/Olde Richmond, about a 15-minute walk from the Market-Frankford Line's Girard stop, or the 15 trolley to Frankford & Delaware right across the street.

top3.title: Marx in Soho by Howard Zinn Featuring Bob Weick
top3.venue: Broken Mirror Studio
top3.why: Howard Zinn's one-man play imagines Karl Marx bargaining his way back from the afterlife to defend himself against 2026 America, delivered by longtime interpreter Bob Weick, who's performed the role hundreds of times worldwide. Sharp, funny, and unapologetically didactic — “the words the billionaire class doesn't want you to hear.” $20; opens tonight and runs most of the week. (No confirmed street address for Broken Mirror Studio — sources disagree between a Broad Street and a North 9th Street location, so confirm before heading out.)

top3.title: Body As an Archive
top3.venue: Icebox Project Space Gallery
top3.why: A former Cirque du Soleil performer's autobiographical solo show tracing a childhood inside a brutal military-style circus training system, from age four to a premiere at nine — framed as reclaiming a body and voice that discipline tried to own. Opens tonight, running three nights. $25; Olde Kensington, about a 10-minute walk from the Market-Frankford Line's Girard stop.

top3.title: Minyo Crusaders / Mariposas Galácticas
top3.venue: PhilaMOCA, 531 N. 12th St, Philadelphia, PA 19123

Classic Wooden Shoe programming: politically engaged literature with a concrete cause attached.

top3.venue: PhilaMOCA, 531 N 12th St, Philadelphia, PA 19123

top3.title: Ray Cappo talks 90’s Krishnacore

He spent six years as a celibate monk before returning to music; expect a genuinely unusual insider account, not a nostalgia set. South Street, easy walk from Center City.

top3.title: IH20: The Big Anniversary Party
top3.venue: Indy Hall Clubhouse at 709 N 2nd St, 709 N 2nd St 3rd Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19123, USA

The party frames it as two decades of showing up for each other rather than just surviving, which tracks with the community's whole ethos: “take care of yourself, take care of each other, take care of this place.” Northern Liberties, near 2nd & Spring Garden, a few blocks from the Market-Frankford Line.

top3.title: Buzzcocks
top3.venue: Underground Arts, 1200 Callowhill St, Philadelphia, PA 19107
top3.why: Buzzcocks — one of the foundational UK punk bands, the ones who basically invented the punk love song — play a WXPN-presented show at Underground Arts. Still touring on the strength of a back catalog that shaped everything from pop-punk to indie rock. 21+, doors 7:00 PM, show 8:00. Callowhill, a couple of blocks from the Broad Street Line's Spring Garden stop.

top3.title: Take Your Shot: A Motivational Seminar with Luigi Mangione
top3.venue: Asian Arts Initiative Black Box Theater
top3.why: Satirical immersive theater staged as a mandatory corporate motivational seminar — fictional “Ramco Laboratories” brings in Luigi Mangione (framed here as a corporate-America folk antihero, not the real defendant in an active criminal case) to inspire employees to “take your shot.” Pointed, uncomfortable, and exactly the kind of anti-corporate satire that doesn't get made by anyone with something to lose. Chinatown North/Callowhill, close to the Broad Street Line's Race-Vine or Spring Garden stops.

top3.title: Moral Injury
top3.venue: First Unitarian Church of Philadelphia
top3.why: Two castaways attempt to hunt and eat a pig with predictably dire results — a genre-blending piece built on heavy movement, mask, and sound work that uses survival-horror absurdity to get at something more serious about trauma and complicity. Fringe programming at First Unitarian Church, better known for its punk shows.
